```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

Most likelihoods have no closed-form maximiser. This file shows Newton–Raphson by hand,
`optim()` with a reparametrisation, standard errors from the Hessian, a likelihood-ratio
test, and three practical problems.

## 1. Gamma model for the aircondit failure times

$y_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim}\text{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta)$ (shape $\alpha$, rate $\beta$):
$\ell(\alpha,\beta)=n\alpha\log\beta-n\log\Gamma(\alpha)+(\alpha-1)\sum\log y_i-\beta\sum y_i$.
For fixed $\alpha$, $\hat\beta(\alpha)=\alpha/\bar y$. Substituting gives the profile score
for $\alpha$:
$S(\alpha)=n\{\log\alpha-\psi(\alpha)-\log\bar y+\overline{\log y}\}$, with
$I(\alpha)=-S'(\alpha)=n\{\psi'(\alpha)-1/\alpha\}$ ($\psi$ = digamma, $\psi'$ = trigamma).

```{r newton}
data(aircondit, package = "boot")
y <- aircondit$hours; n <- length(y)

S <- function(a) n * (log(a) - digamma(a) - log(mean(y)) + mean(log(y)))
I <- function(a) n * (trigamma(a) - 1 / a)

a <- 1                                    # start at the exponential model
iter <- data.frame()
for (k in 0:5) {
  iter <- rbind(iter, data.frame(k = k, alpha = a, score = S(a), info = I(a)))
  a <- a + S(a) / I(a)                    # Newton-Raphson step
}
print(iter, digits = 6)
alpha_hat <- a
beta_hat  <- alpha_hat / mean(y)
c(alpha_hat = alpha_hat, beta_hat = beta_hat)
```

Here $I(\alpha)$ does not depend on the data, so Newton–Raphson and Fisher scoring
take the same steps.

## 2. The same fit with `optim()`

`optim()` minimises, so we pass the negative log-likelihood. Working with
$(\log\alpha,\log\beta)$ keeps both parameters positive with no constraints.

```{r optim}
nll <- function(par) -sum(dgamma(y, shape = exp(par[1]), rate = exp(par[2]), log = TRUE))
fit <- optim(c(0, log(1 / mean(y))), nll, method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE)
fit$convergence                  # 0 = the algorithm reports convergence
exp(fit$par)                     # (alpha_hat, beta_hat)
-fit$value                       # maximised log-likelihood

V_log <- solve(fit$hessian)      # inverse observed information, log scale
se_log <- sqrt(diag(V_log))
se_log
# Delta method: se(alpha_hat) = alpha_hat * se(log alpha_hat)
se_alpha <- exp(fit$par[1]) * se_log[1]
se_alpha
1 / sqrt(I(alpha_hat))           # same, from the profile information
```

## 3. Likelihood-ratio test: exponential ($\alpha=1$) against gamma

```{r lrt}
ll_exp   <- sum(dexp(y, rate = 1 / mean(y), log = TRUE))
ll_gamma <- -fit$value
LR <- 2 * (ll_gamma - ll_exp)
c(ll_exp = ll_exp, ll_gamma = ll_gamma, LR = LR,
  p_value = pchisq(LR, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE))

# Wald test of the same hypothesis
z_wald <- (alpha_hat - 1) / (1 / sqrt(I(alpha_hat)))
c(z = z_wald, p_value = 2 * pnorm(-abs(z_wald)))
```

With 12 observations the data cannot distinguish the exponential from the gamma.

## 4. Practical problem 1: several local maxima (Cauchy location)

```{r cauchy}
yc <- c(-2, -1, 0, 7, 8)
ll_c <- function(t) -sum(log(1 + (yc - t)^2))      # Cauchy location, scale 1
starts <- c(-3, 0, 4, 6, 10)
res <- t(sapply(starts, function(s) {
  o <- optim(s, function(t) -ll_c(t), method = "BFGS")
  c(start = s, theta_hat = o$par, loglik = -o$value, convergence = o$convergence)
}))
round(res, 3)
```

Every run reports convergence, but starts at 6 and 10 stop at a local maximum
with a lower log-likelihood. Use several starting values and keep the best.

```{r cauchy-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
tt <- seq(-5, 12, by = 0.02)
plot(tt, sapply(tt, ll_c), type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "log-likelihood")
rug(yc)
```

## 5. Practical problem 2: an estimate on the boundary

```{r boundary}
n0 <- 20; y0 <- 0                     # no successes in 20 trials
theta_hat0 <- y0 / n0
se0 <- sqrt(theta_hat0 * (1 - theta_hat0) / n0)   # = Ii(theta_hat)^(-1/2), and Ii(0) is infinite
c(theta_hat = theta_hat0, wald_se = se0)           # usual Wald interval is [0, 0]: useless
# The MLE is on the boundary, so it does not solve S(theta) = 0: S(0) = -n0 = -20
# LR interval: l(theta) = 20 log(1 - theta), l(0) = 0, so the upper end solves 20 log(1 - theta) = -1.92
1 - exp(-qchisq(0.95, 1) / 2 / n0)
```

## 6. Practical problem 3: non-identifiability

If $y_i\sim N(a+b,1)$, only $a+b$ is identified: the log-likelihood is flat along the
lines $a+b=c$ and the Hessian is singular.

```{r nonident}
set.seed(2027)
yn <- rnorm(30, mean = 3, sd = 1)
nll_ab <- function(p) -sum(dnorm(yn, mean = p[1] + p[2], sd = 1, log = TRUE))
o1 <- optim(c(0, 0), nll_ab, method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE)
o2 <- optim(c(5, -5), nll_ab, method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE)
rbind(start_00 = c(o1$par, sum = sum(o1$par)), start_5m5 = c(o2$par, sum = sum(o2$par)))
eigen(o1$hessian)$values              # one eigenvalue is 0: no unique maximiser
```
